newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Trade, defence to dominate Australian PM visit.
newsitem.headline: Trade, defence to dominate Australian PM visit.

text.p: Defence and economic issues are expected to dominate Australian Prime Minister John Howard's first visit as head of government to neighbouring New Zealand later this week, a senior Australian official said on Wednesday.
"Trade liberalisation is important in terms of increasing export growth and getting market access to other countries," the official told reporters.
"Australia has gone a long way down that track already and we want movement from everyone," he said.

Howard was due to fly to Wellington on Saturday and will return on Monday. He was scheduled to meet New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger, Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters, key ministers and leading business people, and opposition leader Helen Clark.
Howard was keen to cement ties between Wellington and his conservative Liberal-National government, which swept to power in March 1996, ending 13 years of Labor rule, the official said.
The two countries have similar priorities on trade liberalisation, regional stability, and international trade issues, he said.
New Zealand is Australia's third largest trading partner. Two-way trade in goods and services was A$11.45 billion ($8.7 billion) in the year to June 30, 1996.

Australia and New Zealand, one of Canberra's closest allies, have axed trade barriers between them under their Closer Economic Relations pact, which they are also pushing to link with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations' planned free trade agreement.
Both are key free trade champions within the 18-member Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) forum, which has pledged to abolish trade barriers among the booming Pacific Rim economies by 2020.

The official said he expected the issue of a single aviation market between the two countries to be on the agenda as New Zealand had been lobbying for increased Australian landing rights to better tap into lucrative Asian markets.
The two nations late last year signed a single aviation agreement allowing the countries' airlines to fly within and between both countries without restriction.
However, there are still limits on so-called "beyond rights", preventing New Zealand airlines from taking passengers from Australia to a third country.
"They (New Zealand) are still looking for more beyond rights from Australia and that's something which is being discussed," the official said.
The issue is one of the major sticking points in the creation of a single aviation market between the two neighbours.
The official said defence spending was also expected to feature, with Australia keen to secure new frigate orders from New Zealand's navy.
